name: Open Sesame Burger (Served open-faced on a sesame seed bun)

recipe.history:
Sesame seeds — Sesamum indicum — are among the oldest cultivated oilseed crops in human history, with origins tracing back more than 3,500 years to the Indian subcontinent and the ancient civilizations of Mesopotamia. Archaeological evidence from Harappa and sites along the Indus Valley suggests that sesame was being harvested and pressed for oil as early as 1500 BCE. The crop spread rapidly along ancient trade routes into Egypt, Persia, and China, where it was prized not only for its rich, nutty oil but also for the seeds themselves, which were scattered over breads and flatbreads to add fragrance, texture, and a toasty depth of flavor. In the ancient Middle East, sesame was considered a symbol of immortality — Assyrian legend holds that the gods drank sesame wine the night before they created the earth — and its role in cuisine was nothing short of sacred. By the time the Roman Empire was grinding sesame into condiment pastes, the seed had cemented itself as a cornerstone of global cooking.

Sesame arrived in the Americas via the transatlantic slave trade, carried by enslaved West Africans who called the seeds "benne" and continued cultivating them in the American South, where benne wafers and benne brittle became regional staples. But sesame's most iconic marriage with American cuisine came through the hamburger bun. By the mid-twentieth century, bakers discovered that a crown of sesame seeds on a soft enriched roll gave the bun visual identity, a subtle crunch against the soft crumb, and a layer of toasty, almost buttery flavor that bridged the gap between the bread and the savory beef below. McDonald's standardized it in the 1960s, and from that point forward the sesame seed bun became the universal shorthand for the American hamburger — so ubiquitous, so expected, that it stopped being noticed at all. Bob Belcher notices. Bob has always noticed.

I remember the first time a burger genuinely stopped me in my tracks. It wasn't at some celebrated restaurant — it was at a folding table at a block party, late August, the kind of heat that makes the air smell like cut grass and charcoal. Someone had set a burger in front of me open-faced, both halves of the bun lying flat, and the patty sat on the bottom half like it owned the place, glistening, framed by a crown of toasted sesame seeds that had gone just past golden into something that smelled like a memory I couldn't quite name. I picked it up and ate the bottom half first, then the top, and I understood for the first time that serving a burger open-faced isn't a gimmick — it's an invitation to look at what you've made, to appreciate the architecture before you collapse it. That moment has lived in me ever since, and every time I smell sesame seeds hitting a hot pan I am eight years old again and it is August and everything is exactly right.

There is only one correct internal temperature for a beef patty, and it is medium rare: 130 to 135°F, or 54 to 57°C at the very center. This is not a preference — it is a philosophy grounded in the biology of beef and the chemistry of heat. At medium rare, the myoglobin in the muscle has been warmed but not fully denatured, which means the interior retains its deep, iron-rich, beefy character. The fat has begun to render and baste the surrounding meat from within, keeping every bite juicy and cohesive rather than dry and crumbling. Cooking beyond this point — into medium, medium well, or the culinary crime of well done — is an act of progressive destruction: moisture driven out, fat rendered away entirely, proteins tightened into something closer to shoe leather than food. A well-done burger is an apology. A medium rare burger is a declaration. It tells the person eating it that you respect the animal, respect the craft, and respect their palate enough to give them beef as it was meant to be eaten — pink, warm, yielding, and alive with flavor in a way that no amount of ketchup can compensate for if you've cooked it to death. Medium rare or nothing. There is no argument to be had.
ingredients: 360g (3 cups) bread flour, plus more for dusting
1 egg yolk + 1 tbsp whole milk (for egg wash)
3 tbsp raw sesame seeds (for topping the buns)
680g (1½ lbs) freshly ground beef — 80/20 blend (chuck and short rib, ground once through a coarse die)
½ tsp freshly cracked black pepper
1 tbsp neutral oil (such as grapeseed or canola, for the pan or grill)
2–3 tbsp warm water (to thin to drizzleable consistency)
2 medium beefsteak tomatoes, sliced ¼-inch thick
½ small red onion, very thinly sliced into rings
instructions: 1. MAKE THE BUNS — ACTIVATE YEAST: Combine warm water, warm milk, and sugar in the bowl of a stand mixer. Sprinkle in the yeast and stir gently. Let stand 5–10 minutes until foamy and fragrant, confirming the yeast is active.

2. MAKE THE BUNS — MIX DOUGH: Add the egg, softened butter, and salt to the yeast mixture. Add the bread flour all at once. Mix on low speed with the dough hook until a shaggy dough forms, then increase to medium speed and knead for 8–10 minutes until the dough is smooth, supple, and pulls cleanly away from the bowl sides.

3. MAKE THE BUNS — FIRST RISE: Form the dough into a ball, place in a lightly oiled bowl, and cover with plastic wrap or a damp kitchen towel. Let rise at room temperature until doubled in size, approximately 1 to 1½ hours.

4. MAKE THE BUNS — SHAPE: Punch down the dough and divide into 4 equal portions (approximately 160g each). Shape each into a tight, smooth ball by pulling the surface taut and pinching the seam underneath. Place on a parchment-lined baking sheet, spaced 3 inches apart. Press each ball gently to flatten into a disk roughly 3½ inches in diameter.
5. MAKE THE BUNS — SECOND RISE: Cover loosely with plastic wrap and let proof until noticeably puffed and jiggly, about 45–60 minutes. Preheat your oven to 375°F / 190°C during this time.

6. MAKE THE BUNS — SEED AND BAKE: Whisk the egg yolk with the tablespoon of milk and brush the tops and sides of each bun generously. Immediately scatter sesame seeds liberally over the tops, pressing very lightly so they adhere. Bake for 17–20 minutes, rotating the pan once at the halfway mark, until the buns are deep golden brown and the sesame seeds are fragrant and toasted. Transfer to a wire rack and cool completely before slicing.

7. MAKE THE SESAME SAUCE: In a small bowl, whisk together the tahini, toasted sesame oil, soy sauce, rice wine vinegar, honey, grated garlic, and white pepper. Add warm water one tablespoon at a time, whisking until the sauce is smooth, glossy, and thin enough to drizzle freely. Taste and adjust — add more vinegar for brightness, more honey for sweetness, more soy for depth. Set aside.

8. PREP TOPPINGS: Slice the tomatoes and season lightly with flaky salt. Separate the red onion into individual rings and place in a small bowl of ice water for 10 minutes to crisp them and mellow their bite, then drain and pat dry. Wash and dry the butter lettuce leaves. Slice the cornichons lengthwise if large.

9. FORM AND TEMPER THE PATTIES: Divide the ground beef into 4 portions (about 170g / 6 oz each). Handle the meat as little as possible — work quickly and with cold hands. Gently shape each portion into a patty approximately ¾ inch thick and slightly wider than the bun diameter to account for shrinkage. Press a shallow dimple into the center of each patty with your thumb to prevent doming during cooking. Season aggressively with kosher salt and cracked black pepper on both sides immediately before cooking. Do not season early.

10. COOK THE PATTIES TO MEDIUM RARE: Heat a heavy cast-iron skillet or griddle over high heat until it begins to smoke lightly. Add the neutral oil and swirl to coat. Place the patties dimple-side up in the pan, pressing gently once to ensure full contact. Cook undisturbed for 3–4 minutes until a deep mahogany crust forms on the bottom. Flip once. Cook an additional 2–3 minutes. Check the internal temperature using an instant-read thermometer inserted through the side of the patty into the center — you are looking for exactly 130–135°F / 54–57°C for medium rare. Remove the patties from the heat and rest on a wire rack for 3–4 minutes. The carryover will bring them to the ideal serving temperature. Do not cook beyond 135°F.

11. TOAST THE BUNS: While the patties rest, slice the cooled sesame buns in half horizontally. Place both halves cut-side down in the same hot skillet (with residual fat) for 60–90 seconds until golden and lightly crisped. Remove and place open-faced on serving plates — bottom half and top half side by side, cut-side up.

12. ASSEMBLE OPEN-FACED: On the bottom bun half, lay a leaf or two of butter lettuce so it slightly overhangs the edge. Layer 2–3 tomato slices over the lettuce. Place the rested medium rare patty directly on the tomatoes. Drizzle a generous zigzag of sesame sauce over the top of the patty, letting it run down the sides. Arrange a few red onion rings and the cornichon slices over the sauced patty. Scatter a pinch of toasted sesame seeds over everything. Finish with a small pinch of flaky sea salt.

13. PLATE AND SERVE: Place the dressed bottom-half beside the top bun half (plain side down, sesame seed side up) on the same plate so the burger presents fully open-faced. Serve immediately — medium rare beef waits for no one.
